task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper news story for general readers. Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of May 8, 2025. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: Clearwater National Laboratory officially began operations on May 8, 2025, of Helios-2, a computing system rated at 4.8 exaflops, making it the fastest publicly accessible supercomputer in the world at the time of launch.
An exaflop is one quintillion (10 to the 18th power) mathematical operations per second; Helios-2 is nearly three times faster than the previous U.S. national laboratory record holder.
Helios-2 is housed in a 12,000-square-meter facility in Sandover, New Mexico, and draws up to 42 megawatts of power at peak load.
The system uses 9,400 next-generation accelerator chips developed by chipmaker Tessera Systems under a $2.1 billion contract with the Department of Energy.

Clearwater director Dr. Chioma Bankole said: "Helios-2 allows us to simulate physical processes at a resolution and timescale that was simply impossible before. Climate, materials, biology — the questions we can now ask have changed."

The first allocated research projects include a global climate model running at 1-kilometer atmospheric resolution, a protein folding study of membrane-bound receptors, and a fusion plasma turbulence simulation.

Half of Helios-2's compute time has been reserved for unclassified open-science projects selected through a competitive peer-review process; the other half is allocated to Department of Energy mission programs.
Bankole said open-science allocations were oversubscribed by a factor of six: the laboratory received requests for 28 exaflop-hours and can award 4.8 exaflop-hours in the first year.
Helios-2's cooling system uses direct liquid cooling for the processor nodes; the waste heat will supply a geothermal heat loop that warms adjacent laboratory buildings.
The system requires approximately 440,000 liters of deionized water per day for cooling; the laboratory uses water recycled through a closed-loop system.
Total project cost was $3.7 billion, including the facility construction, the compute hardware, and a 10-year maintenance contract.
China's Taishan-3 supercomputer, rated at 5.2 exaflops, is faster but is not publicly accessible; Helios-2 is the fastest system available to international research applicants.
The TOP500 list, which ranks the world's fastest supercomputers biannually, will include Helios-2 in its November 2025 edition.
Dr. Bankole said the laboratory plans to accept international researcher allocation requests beginning in September 2025.

The 42-megawatt peak power draw is equivalent to the consumption of approximately 35,000 U.S. households; Clearwater Lab will source 100% of its power from renewables under a long-term purchase agreement.
Seven university research teams that participated in the previous-generation system at Clearwater have already received Helios-2 allocations.
The Department of Energy said Helios-2 was essential for modeling nuclear stockpile performance, though that work falls within the classified half of compute time.
Tessera Systems CEO Marcus Webb said the Helios-2 contract accelerated the company's chip development roadmap by approximately 18 months.
Dr. Bankole said the laboratory trained a 240-person operations staff specifically for Helios-2 over the past two years.
The previous Clearwater record holder, Helios-1, was decommissioned to make room for the new system; its processors are being refurbished for use in regional university computing clusters.

a compute speed different from 4.8 exaflops
a confirmed scientific result from the system
